challenges.name: idempotent-progress-quiz
challenges.title: Which part of progress is idempotent?
challenges.description: Two fixes proposed after progress went from 80% back to 40% and a learner got two certificates: a GREATEST update, and an event table that remembers every eventId.

questions.explanation: False. GREATEST makes the stored progress idempotent: the retry cannot lower or change the percent. But the certificate is a side effect, and this code runs it after every event that finds the course at 100%, including the retry of ev_802 and any later stale event for that course. Exactly-once needs its own guard: publish only when this event moved the course from below 100 to 100, remember processed eventIds, and in the database a unique constraint on certificates (user_id, course_id) as the last line of defence. The misconception is that an idempotent state update makes everything that follows it idempotent too.

True. The primary key makes the second INSERT of the same event_id wait for the first transaction. When the first commits, the second sees the conflict, does nothing and returns no row, so it answers duplicate without touching progress. If the first rolled back, the second would insert and process the event, which is also correct: the event then counts exactly once. This is why the eventId check belongs in the same transaction as the update, enforced by a key, and not in a separate SELECT before it, which two concurrent deliveries could both pass. The misconception is that an in-memory or SELECT-then-INSERT check gives the same guarantee across several API instances.

challenges.name: idempotent-progress-service
challenges.title: ProgressService: duplicates, late events and one completion
challenges.description:
The CodeDev mobile app sends a progress event while a learner reads or watches a lesson: { eventId, userId, courseId, lessonId, percent }. It keeps unsent events in an offline queue and retries a request after a timeout, so the same event can arrive twice and an older event can arrive after a newer one. The shipped ProgressService stored the last value it received, so a slow older event moved a lesson from 80% back to 40%, and a retried final event issued a second completion certificate. Write ProgressService.record(event) so that progress never goes backwards and the completion is published exactly once. Its stores are injected through the constructor: in-memory fakes here, PostgreSQL tables in production.

Rules. Invalid: eventId and userId must be non-empty strings, catalog.lessonIds(courseId) must return a list that contains lessonId, and percent must be an integer from 0 to 100 (the events come from JSON, so check the values at runtime). Otherwise return { status: "invalid" } and change nothing - do not remember its eventId. Duplicate: processed.has(eventId) -> { status: "duplicate" }, nothing changes. Stale: percent is not higher than the stored percent of that lesson (a lesson with nothing stored counts as 0) -> { status: "stale", lessonPercent: <stored>, coursePercent }. Applied: otherwise store the percent -> { status: "applied", lessonPercent, coursePercent, courseCompleted }. Every valid event, applied or stale, is remembered with processed.add(eventId). coursePercent is Math.floor(sum of the stored percents of every lesson of the course / number of lessons), with missing lessons counted as 0. When an event moves coursePercent from below 100 to 100, call bus.publish({ type: "course.completed", userId, courseId }) once and return courseCompleted: true; in every other case courseCompleted is false and nothing is published.

Input (stdin): { "courses": { courseId: lessonId[] }, "progress"?: [[userId, courseId, lessonId, percent]], "processed"?: [eventId], "events": [event], "summary"?: true }. progress and processed describe the state before the first event (for example, events stored before a restart). Output: one line per event with its status and percentages, the published events, and the stored percent of every lesson per learner and course; with summary, the count per status, the number of published events, the number of stored lessons and the sum of their percents. Do not change the types, the stores or the test runner.
hints: For one incoming event, what has to be true for it to change anything at all - and among the events that do change something, which single one is allowed to announce that the course is finished?

Look at three moments: before anything is stored (is the event valid, has its eventId been seen), the comparison between the incoming percent and the stored one, and the course percentage computed before and after the store. The completion depends on both of those course percentages, not only on the one after.

The same shape for a reading streak: events { eventId, day } where the streak may only grow. Event r1 day 5 on a stored day 3 -> stored 5, applied; r0 day 4 arriving late -> stays 5, stale; r1 again -> duplicate. A 7-day badge is awarded when the streak goes from 6 to 7, so a later event that finds the streak at 9 awards nothing, and neither does a retry.
